catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress in Umanakaina is predictable and therefore not phonemic for all but three-syllable words. Two-syllable words always carry the stress on the fist syllable. For three-syllable words, stress on the penultimate syllable contrasts with stress on the first syllable as follows: kokára 'type of ritual' sisíya 'talking' wagúra 'craw-fish sp.' kókara 'fish sp.' sísiya 'ants' wágura 'yam sp.' ... Conventions: Orthographic Phonemic stress is not written.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; in trisyllables stress is lexically either initial or penultimate (minimal pairs exist), so stress is contrastive only in three-syllable words; the source calls stress otherwise 'predictable' but gives no explicit rule for words of four or more syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Three-syllable words are the stated exception to predictability (initial vs penultimate contrast: kokára/kókara, sisíya/sísiya, wagúra/wágura). Evensen 1993:14 adds that the penultimate-stressed trisyllabic class selects the locative clitic allomorph /-i.ya/ (tawáiya 'in his house' vs watéya 'in his place').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated lexical items with acute marks); no statement about phrase-level prominence. 4-page draft OPD 'posted as is without peer review'; the fuller primary analysis is the unpublished Evensen & Evensen 1982 phonemes ms.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is titled 'Umanakaina (Gwedena) Language [GDN]', Bonenepi village, Rabaraba, Milne Bay Province; Evensen 1993 states the analysis is based on the 'Main Dialect' as defined in Jesudason & Jesudason 1991 dialect survey. Dutton 1975:643 notes two dialects of Gwedena (upper Ugu vs. the rest) and equates Gwedena with Capell's 'Umanakaina'. Same languoid as uman1240; no separate dialect glottocode needed.

sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals': stress predictable (non-phonemic) except in three-syllable words; disyllables always initial stress; in trisyllables penultimate vs initial stress contrasts (kokára 'type of ritual' vs kókara 'fish sp.', sisíya/sísiya, wagúra/wágura). Orthography: 'Phonemic stress is not written.' Nothing said about words of 4+ syllables or secondary stress.

sources.note: No general stress rule; sec. IX (p.14): words that, inflected with 3SG.POSS, 'become three syllable words with stress on the penultimate syllable' take clitic form /-i.ya/, otherwise /-e.ya/; stressed vocoids marked in the examples (scan, scanned at 300 dpi). Confirms stress is lexically relevant in trisyllables. Refers to Evensen & Evensen 1982 phonemes ms. and 1986 Grammar Essentials p.91.
